newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union in escalating strike against GM.
newsitem.headline: Canada union in escalating strike against GM.

text.p: More than 15,000 unionized workers at General Motors Corp.'s Canadian unit were off the job on Thursday after beginning a strike late Wednesday that could shut down all GM Canada operations by Oct. 9.

The union began a so-called "escalating" strike against GM less than two hours before Wednesday's midnight strike deadline, after GM delivered a last-minute economic package that Canadian Auto Workers president Buzz Hargrove called an "insult."
"So we are on strike," Hargrove said. "Our plants are down."
Talks were continuing on Thursday in Toronto, but Hargrove said the two sides remain "worlds apart" on the major issue of outsourcing and a various work time and work rule issues.

The strike immediately halted production at GM's Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste-Therese, Quebec, assembly plants. Other GM Canada facilities will join the strike starting on Oct. 6 and all Canadian operations will be shut down by Oct. 9 if no deal is reached.
Analysts said last week that a full strike by the company's 26,000 unionized workers in Canada could cost GM $100 million to $150 million a week.

The CAW has said its C$50 million ($36.5 million) strike fund could last up to eight weeks and stretch to 16 weeks under a new credit facility. The union has also set a special strike dues convention for Oct. 18 to raise funds from the entire 210,000 membership of the CAW.
Hargrove said GM's last-minute economic offer was an insult to the union and a "total joke" crafted by executives at GM headquarters in Detroit.
He said he gave GM Canada chief negotiator Dean Munger the "opportunity to withdraw" the offer before the union's caucus meeting at 10 a.m. Thursday (1400 GMT).

Munger said the strike would have a "severe impact" on GM Canada's operations, but he declined to speculate when the impact would reach U.S. operations or cripple the just-in-time parts supply strategy.
He acknowledged the union's rejection of the economic package, but would not comment on why the offer had been made only hours before the strike deadline.
"They indicated they weren't happy with it," he said, ducking into an elevator. "We're going to go back and re-evaluate their comments."
GM said earlier that a strike in Canada will not affect talks with the United Auto Workers in the United States.
"We're working pretty much independently," said GM spokesman Gerry Holmes.
